Design Palette

Design Book

1,220 sq ft · 2 bed / 3 bath

A black-and-white checkerboard floor, set on the diagonal, runs through the entire home — bedrooms, both upstairs bathrooms, living room, kitchen, dining room, entryways, closets — at one consistent size throughout, stopping only at the downstairs bath, where a small-format alabaster mosaic takes the whole floor, paired with blue-green tiled walls and matte black hardware. The primary bedroom gets a pair of twin beds, plus a power recline love seat. The secondary bedroom gets full bed. The downstairs powder room is converted into a full bath laid out as a two-column curbless wet room, and the living room gets a matching power recline sofa and storage coffee table.

A note on flexibility. The one must-have is the checkerboard tile throughout. Everything else — colors, materials, fixtures, and how to get the best value — is genuinely open to the design firm's judgment. This palette is a starting reference, not a locked spec. The general aesthetic direction we're after: fresh and current, the kind of space that photographs well today, but grounded enough in timeless choices that it won't read as dated in five or ten years.
By Room Material callouts and specifications
Primary Bedroom

Two separate twin beds give the kids who sleep here their own space. A power recline sleeper love seat sits between them for guests. The 13-foot wall behind both headboards and the sofa is wrapped floor to ceiling in the same wood-look plank tile used on the entryway wall, run vertically in 13 columns to pull the eye up — a durable, wipeable surface right where beds and furniture make contact. Checkerboard floor, gray walls in glossy finish elsewhere in the room. Closets stay open — doors come off, frames stay in place — fitted with built-in organizers and a built-in desktop. All hardware in matte black.

Primary Bathroom

Alcove tub / tile shower with matte black drain kit, right drain, and a curved shower curtain rod. Sea-glass ceramic in a wavy glossy glaze — Lilah, Opal, set in a straight 6" grid — wraps the tub surround and carries straight on down the whole wall that holds the vanity and toilet, floor to ceiling — one continuous plane rather than a patch behind the mirror. Single 36" vanity, Acorn finish, black hardware provides unobstructed width to the tub's full alcove opening. Checkerboard floor, gray walls, matte black faucet, medicine cabinet, toilet, shower head + handheld wand for tub use.

Dining Room

Checkerboard floors, gray walls in glossy finish. Kitchen cabinets and counters extend across the length of the dining room with 36" counter depth to allow use as desk space at bar stool height and space to put a coffee machine. Dining table is 36" round dining table (white marble top, matte black base), paired with 4 black ash dining chairs. The existing slider is replaced with a matte black aluminum bi-fold door — three panels that fold away to open the wall to the patio.

Downstairs Bathroom

Powder room converted to a full bath: a curbless two-column wet room, floor-to-ceiling Lilah, Opal tile on the wet column's three walls. The 31" west column is the shower, sloping to a full-length linear drain; the 30" east column keeps the toilet dry behind a fixed glass panel. Ceiling-mount rain head 17" off the south wall, valve below it, a recessed nook on the same line — no handheld wand, since a rain head throws the least spray of any head type. St. Tropez corner sink in the NW corner with a matte black Kohler Elate faucet and a mirror/cabinet above it, facing into the room rather than the shower. Same Kingston toilet as elsewhere. Entry is a 24" pocket door, satin black.

Drawn to scale, actual 61" x 61" room. Curbless: the floor slopes to a full-length linear drain, so the shower keeps its full 31" clear width — CPC 408.5's 30" circle passes and the toilet column is 30" exact. The fixed glass panel and floor slope keep the dry side dry. St. Tropez corner sink, ceiling rain head 17" off the south wall, recessed nook on the same line. 24" pocket door on the east wall; TP holder, towel bar, and three hooks as shown.

Entryway

An archway passageway wall between the living room and kitchen. A tiled accent wall — wood-look ribbed ceramic in a plank format — wraps up and over the small ceiling section above it, reading as one clean, continuous statement; the long run of wall is exactly what the plank proportion and relief texture need to shine. Optional: a shoe storage bench along the wall. Checkerboard floors, gray walls elsewhere in the room.

Appendix Bathroom wall tile options
Bathroom Wall Tile Options

Five wall tile options compared for the three bathrooms — on reflectance, price, format, and how each pairs with the Leona checkerboard floor (white squares ≈85% reflectance, black squares ≈16%, both warm in undertone despite reading as neutral). Lilah, Opal is the tile now specified throughout this book — the third pick, after Jaden, Hunter (the original) and Mila, Jade, and cheaper than both. The price and format deltas below are still quoted against Hunter, the original baseline.

Layout impact—

Deep emerald, true green, glossy. Darkest of the five options.

Against the checkerboard: At 18% it sits almost exactly on Nero Marquina's own value — only 2 points apart (+2 / −67 to the white squares) — and its 134° blue-emerald hue runs cooler than the floor's warm undertone.

Dax Forest
6" x 24" · matte porcelain
CONSIDERED
Reflectance · 41.2%
Hue / saturation94.4°, 23.6% sat
Price$5.22 / sq ft (−60% vs. Hunter)

Layout impactDifferent scale — large plank, matte not glossy

Cheapest by a wide margin, nearly Mila's exact hue. Matte finish and a much bigger plank than Hunter's — the boldest single element in the room if used.

Against the checkerboard: At 41% it clears the black squares comfortably (+25 / −44), but matte against a matte floor flattens the sheen contrast, and a 6"x24" plank is bolder than the floor's own 12" checkers.

Price$19.97 / sq ft (+54% vs. Hunter)

Closest match to Hunter's own proportions (same width, just shorter pieces), so the vertical-column look translates most directly. Priciest of the five.

Against the checkerboard: At 43% it clears both extremes (+27 / −42) with the warmest hue of the five (100°). Matte, so it loses Hunter's glossy sheen against the floor — but its 2.5" width means the room's column composition carries over most directly.

Lilah Opal
6" x 6" · glossy ceramic
SPECIFIED
Reflectance · 49.0%
Hue / saturation163.4°, 16.5% sat
Price$8.94 / sq ft (−31% vs. Hunter)
Box$124.22 / 13.89 sf
Layout impactDifferent scale — 6" square, not a plank

Added after spotting it installed: strong piece-to-piece shade variation — pale sage squares scattered among blue-teals — under a wavy high-gloss glaze. The coolest hue on this page (163°, past even Hunter's 134°), leaning teal rather than jade. Cheapest after Dax.

Against the checkerboard: At 49% it sits comfortably between the black and white squares (+33 / −36), nearly as balanced as Mila — but its cool teal hue pulls against the floor's warm undertone, where Mila leans with it.

Mila Jade
4" x 4" · glossy ceramic
CONSIDERED
Reflectance · 54.1%
Hue / saturation92.1°, 16.6% sat
Price$10.38 / sq ft (−20% vs. Hunter)
Box$132.90 / 12.8 sf
Layout impactDifferent scale — small square, not a plank

Lightest of the five options and glossy. Warmer hue than Hunter (92° vs 134°), closer to the floor's own warm undertone.

Against the checkerboard: At 54% it lands almost exactly halfway between the checkerboard's black and white squares (+38 / −31) — a genuine third value, not a near-match to either extreme — and it stays glossy, keeping the glossy-wall/matte-floor sheen contrast.

Summary. Hunter is the darkest option on this page and runs cooler than the checkerboard floor's warm marbling. Mila is the lightest of the five, keeps a glossy finish, and its warm hue sits closest to the floor's own undertone, though it's a small square rather than a plank. Dax is the least expensive by far but matte and a much larger plank. Ellie keeps Hunter's plank width most closely but is matte and the most expensive per square foot. Lilah, added after it was spotted installed, is nearly as balanced as Mila in value and second-cheapest, but reads teal — the coolest hue of the five, pulling against the floor's warm undertone. Seen installed, it won the spec anyway: the variation is the look, and only Dax costs less. Each carries a different trade-off among reflectance, price, format, and finish.
